title: Nomen et omen
sentences: In January of 1848, no one had the slightest notion that they might even see war before the year was out.
The humane patriots thought of everything in the world except manufacturing gunpowder, and if somewhere during a noisier administrative reshuffle a noble cousin had his head pierced,
the press had three weeks in which to debate the unheard-of bloodshed most entertainingly, pro and con.
In those days the newspapers and periodicals spoke much of a magnetic somnambulist lady from Vác,
who foretold many wonders, some of which did indeed come to pass to the public's amazement.
Thus she prophesied that one day Komárom would sink beneath the waters.
Poor city—it would have fared well if a modest subsidence might have saved it from its troubles.
The fate that followed outdid the prophecy itself with wretched consequences.
She also foretold that cholera would visit the country, and that those carried off by it would be the luckiest.
When Mór Perczel was elected a deputy and, travelling to Pressburg, was obliged to spend a night in Vác, some acquaintances there so filled his ears with all the somnambulist's wonders
that he finally took a fancy to know the mysterious being at close hand, and was led to her.
By the dim light of a lamp lay the nervous invalid, a very young maiden, her face whiter than any I have ever seen, almost transparent and very thin.
Her eyes, which were very large and clear blue, she never fully opened, and her lips and hands trembled without cease.
Her doctor was present.
Magnetic treatment had been prescribed for the suffering girl against terrible heart spasms, and for six weeks now the magnetic trance had held her.
She was awake only very rarely, slept even more rarely; her normal state was something between dream and waking,
an unceasing unconscious reverie, a vivid feeling of others' joy and pain, without the least awareness of self.
The doctor stepped up to her.
As soon as he entered the girl's extended magnetic aura, sympathetic influence opened her eyes.
She stared straight into her doctor's eyes, her eyelids unmoving.
When the doctor took the girl's hand, a frosty sleepwalker's smile passed over her white face and her trembling ceased.
Then from a distance, barely touching her with his fingertips, the doctor began to stroke the girl's face, forehead, arms,
her breast, slowly and smoothly at first, then faster, in broken strokes, while keeping his eyes fixed intently on her face.
The girl did not move; only her eyelashes seemed to struggle against the irresistible spell that ever gained power over her, closing and opening again.
The pupil unusually dilated.
Gradually her whole face changed wondrously.
An indescribable sweet pain was expressed in her features.
She sighed, wept, her lips parted again and again, until at last a calm smile settled on her face; her head fell back on the cushion of her armchair and she fell asleep.
The doctor then led Mór Perczel into the magnetic aura as well.
At that moment the girl's face took on a grave, exalted, mysterious look.
Who is this man?
the doctor asked her in a soft, familiar tone.
The girl answered after a pause, hesitatingly.
One of the greatest generals of the future.
Perczel smiled and thought to himself: in the camp of parliament, no doubt.
Not in parliament, the girl answered the unspoken thought.
On the battlefield.
And what fate awaits him there?
asked the doctor.
Let him beware of his own name…
By the end of that same year Mór Perczel was a Hungarian general: he fought battles, wrote bulletins, captured armies,
and was counted among the bravest commanders, without the girl from Vác ever once crossing his mind.
It was the thirtieth of December when he accepted battle and lost it.
To this day no one is clear about why that battle was accepted or how it turned out.
It is enough—indeed more than enough—that the battle was lost.
His army was shattered, his guns taken, his position seized.
The flower of his warriors, the splendid Zrínyi battalion, was slaughtered or captured.
When he appeared in Pest after the lost battle, one of the jest-ready judges said to him with no small schadenfreude:
Brother, Mór, your wager wasn't a very lucky one.
Indeed, said the general, without taking offence at the jest—
it just occurs to me that the Vác somnambulist almost predicted this to me a year ago.
If I did not now know that Görgey was the reason I lost the battle, I should believe there was witchcraft in it.
Well, the German too shall have his day yet!
After this defeat they had to leave Pest.
The government and the mint went to Debrecen, and Perczel was charged with escorting them there.
He did so, and after writing them a few letters from Karcag that they did not hang out of their window,
he had second thoughts and turned back to seek out the enemy, who had very prudently halted at Szolnok and was waiting for warmer weather.
One fine misty morning Perczel crossed the ice of the Tisza where he could nearest reach the enemy, began to beat him, and the enemy fell back on Cegléd.
Perczel after him.
The imperial armies were just marching through the vineyards of a village; Perczel still saw the last dragoon vanish among the acacia trees,
and he spurred his horse and ordered his army forward so as not to let them escape.
Meanwhile a small grey-bearded, hawk-nosed man rides up beside him in a frock coat and, without any introduction, tugs at the general's surcoat and addresses him in French:
Do not go that way!
The general looked at him.
He could not imagine what possessed this wild stranger to cling so to his surcoat.
But why should I not go?
The enemy means to lure you into a trap.
I should like to see that!
You shall see it; behind those vineyards hidden batteries must surely be posted, from which they will catch you in crossfire.
What makes you think so?
That follows from the nature of the position.
Pshaw, who can think of everything!
cried the general, shaking the importunate man from his neck, and with that he drew his sword and galloped forward.
After me!
They were hardly a thousand paces from the tangled vineyards when they found a wailing Swabian by the roadside,
who, trying to turn his wagon aside from the charging guns, had luckily driven it with its load into the ditch and was now shouting over his loss.
What village is this, good man?
asked the general of the aggrieved party out of pure curiosity.
Percel!
he replied, scratching his head.
That is me, said the general.
But I want to know what this village is called.
Why, it is called Percel, your Excellency, since the beginning of the world.
The general stopped his horse.
But now the somnambulist's words came back to him.
He turned back, searching with his eyes for the unknown grey-haired man.
He was there, mingled among his escort.
So you truly believe that behind those vineyards there are hidden batteries?
I consider it certain.
The slightest tactical knowledge would reveal it.
So according to this the position is impregnable?
Not quite.
In such cases one usually avoids it.
But that requires very swift movements, and our infantry is already exhausted.
It can be helped; entrust me with a battalion of infantry and two squadrons of cavalry,
and wait here in ambush until I start the game from its lair.
Do it, said the general, and waited to see what the little grey man would do.
He had the infantry climb into the hussars' stirrups and with the utmost precision led them behind the woods.
The idea was as natural as Columbus's egg, and yet no one had thought of it before.
A few minutes later the rapid fire of the infantry that had reached the spot could already be heard behind the vineyards,
and soon one could see the startled batteries withdrawing from both sides.
If Perczel did not shrink back at his own name, there they would again be smashed to pieces.
Thus, leaving the command in other hands—hands to whom the name was no ill omen—he won the battle.
Having driven the enemy from his position, the little grey-haired man returned to the general,
his face all powder smoke; those who went with him could not praise enough his coolness and courage.
I owe you great thanks, said Perczel to the grey stranger, not ashamed to acknowledge his superiority.
May I know who you are?
I, replied the grey man coldly, I am Henry Dembiński.
Perczel, with modest recognition, held out to him the general's baton:
This belongs to you.
Let me henceforth be a common soldier in your army.
